content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a series of guidelines and recommendations to address various aspects of public health, particularly focusing on the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care of HIV and related conditions. Below is a detailed explanation of the key points and recommendations: 1. Introduction of HPV Vaccines: WHO has published a guide to assist countries in integrating the HPV vaccine into their national immunization programs. This guide emphasizes scaling up vaccine introduction and provides lessons learned from real-world applications. 2. Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs): Since the release of WHO's 2016 guidelines for treating gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, and genital herpes, regional workshops have been conducted to disseminate these guidelines. These workshops involved representatives from 22 countries in the Western Pacific, South-East Asia, and Eastern Mediterranean regions, 12 countries in the Americas, and 28 countries in Africa. Some countries, such as Cambodia and Myanmar, have revised their national STI guidelines based on WHO recommendations. Brazil and Cambodia have allocated national funding for gonorrhea antimicrobial resistance surveillance to inform treatment recommendations. Kenya and Zimbabwe have updated their STI treatment protocols in line with WHO guidelines and antimicrobial resistance data. 3. HIV Overview: HIV is a virus that weakens the immune system, making the body more susceptible to infections and certain cancers. It is transmitted through bodily fluids such as blood, breast milk, semen, and vaginal secretions. The most advanced stage of HIV infection is AIDS, for which there is currently no cure or vaccine. 4. HIV Among Adolescents: Adolescents represent a significant proportion of the global HIV burden, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. In 2017, girls in eastern and southern Africa accounted for two-thirds of new HIV infections among young people, driven by gender inequalities, violence, and limited access to education and economic opportunities. Adolescents living with HIV face higher mortality rates compared to children and adults, with AIDS-related deaths among adolescents aged 15–19 continuing to rise. Prevention strategies, such as comprehensive sexuality education, condom distribution, HIV testing, and PrEP, are critical for reducing new infections among adolescents. 5. HIV Testing and Treatment: WHO recommends community-based approaches to improve treatment adherence and retention in care for adolescents living with HIV. Health facilities should provide accessible HIV testing and counseling services, with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care. 6. Antiretroviral Therapy (ART): ART should be initiated in all adolescents living with HIV, regardless of their clinical stage or CD4 cell count. First-line ART regimens should include two nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors plus either a non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor or an integrase strand transfer inhibitor. For adolescents with advanced HIV disease, rapid initiation of ART (within seven days of diagnosis) is recommended. 7. HIV Self-Testing and Partner Notification: HIV self-testing allows individuals to collect their own specimens, perform the test, and interpret the results in private. This approach should be voluntary and accompanied by counseling and referral information. Partner notification services involve trained providers assisting individuals living with HIV in notifying their sexual or drug-injecting partners and offering them HIV testing. 8. Co-Infections and Opportunistic Infections: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for adolescents with HIV to prevent opportunistic infections, particularly in settings with high prevalence of malaria or bacterial infections. In low-prevalence settings, prophylaxis may be discontinued for stable adolescents with suppressed viral loads. 9. Adolescent-Friendly Health Services: Health-care workers should be trained to provide adolescent-friendly services that improve treatment adherence and retention in care. 10. HIV Prevention for Key Populations: WHO emphasizes the importance of targeted interventions for key populations, including men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals. These interventions include harm reduction, condom distribution, and access to PrEP. 11. Sexual and Reproductive Health for Women with HIV: WHO provides guidance on integrating sexual and reproductive health services with HIV care to address the specific needs of women living with HIV. This includes creating an enabling environment and addressing gender inequalities. 12. Response to Sexual Abuse: WHO has developed clinical guidelines for providing trauma-informed care to children and adolescents who have experienced sexual abuse. These guidelines cover post-rape care, psychological support, and good practices for medical examinations. 13. Public Health Response to HIV Drug Resistance: WHO has issued recommendations to address pre-treatment resistance to antiretroviral drugs, emphasizing the importance of surveillance and tailored treatment strategies. 14. Integration of TB and HIV Services: Collaborative TB and HIV services should be integrated into comprehensive care packages, particularly for people who inject drugs. This includes addressing co-infections, mental health needs, and substance use disorders. 15. Monitoring and Surveillance: WHO recommends the use of unique identifiers to link individuals across health services and improve monitoring of HIV care and treatment outcomes. Routine data collection should inform programmatic and policy decisions. These guidelines collectively aim to improve the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care of HIV and related conditions, with a particular focus on vulnerable populations such as adolescents, women, and key populations at higher risk of infection.
